cr-1:
Don't approve it on the spot, and don't walk away either. An ask this far above max usually points to a level or range problem first.

**1. Check the level.** The most common reason a strong candidate prices above max is that they'd be doing next-level work. Compare their experience to your written level definitions, not their current title. If they genuinely fit the next level, hire them there, in that range. Don't up-level just to unlock the money; that breaks leveling for everyone after them.

**2. Check the range.** What survey and cut is it built on, and what's its effective date? If the data is more than a year old, or recruiters keep running into the max for this role, the range is probably the problem. Re-price it by job content, aged to today. If the market moved, your incumbents are underpaid too.

**3. Check internal equity.** Put the offer next to the incumbents in the same job and level. If the new hire would earn well above a peer with similar experience and performance, you're creating a gap you may have to justify later, and if it runs along gender or race lines, that's equal-pay exposure.

**4. If level and range hold, use the other levers:**
- Offer at or near max and explain when the range is next reviewed
- Bridge part of the gap with a one-time sign-on bonus, which doesn't permanently move base
- Adjust the equity grant, if it fits inside your annual share budget
- Commit to an early review against defined outcomes, only if you'll actually honor it

**5. If you still go above max, write it down.** Record a job-related reason (specific relevant experience, documented scarcity for this skill set), get approval at the level your exception policy requires, and treat them as a red circle: future increases come as lump sums until the range catches up. "They asked for more" won't hold up on its own.

**Two guardrails:**
- Don't anchor to their current salary or ask what it is. Many US states and cities ban pay-history questions, and the EU directive does too. Work from the range and their qualifications.
- If the role was posted with a range, an offer well outside it can undercut the "good-faith range" requirement in some jurisdictions. Compensation view, not legal advice (as of 2026-10-23); confirm with employment counsel.

Share the level, the range's source and date, and incumbent pay, and I'll recommend a path.
cr-2:
Compensation view, not legal advice, as of 2026-10-23. Confirm each point with counsel, country by country.

**What it is.** Directive (EU) 2023/970 enforces equal pay for men and women doing the same work or work of equal value, mainly through transparency. "Pay" means base plus all variable and in-kind elements. It covers public and private employers and protects workers (including part-time, fixed-term and agency workers) and job applicants.

**When it applies.** It binds employers through national law. Member states had to transpose it by **7 June 2026**, so what applies to you is each country's implementing law and its effective dates. Transposition has been uneven, so check each country rather than assuming. Most duties apply regardless of size; reporting depends on headcount.

**Before hiring**
- Give applicants the starting pay or range, set on objective, gender-neutral criteria, in the vacancy notice or before the interview
- No pay-history questions; gender-neutral job titles and notices

**For employees**
- Make pay-setting and progression criteria easily accessible (member states may exempt employers under 50 workers from the progression part)
- Answer requests, in writing within **two months**, for a worker's own pay level and average pay levels by sex for workers doing the same work or work of equal value; remind all workers of this right every year
- No contract terms stopping workers from disclosing their pay

**Equal value needs a job evaluation.** Group workers into categories using skills, effort, responsibility and working conditions. This is where most employers have the most work to do.

**Gender pay gap reporting**

| Workers | First report | Then |
|---|---|---|
| 250+ | 7 June 2027 | Every year |
| 150–249 | 7 June 2027 | Every 3 years |
| 100–149 | 7 June 2031 | Every 3 years |

Indicators include mean and median gaps, variable-pay gaps, the share of each sex receiving variable pay, quartile composition, and gaps by category of workers. Countries may extend reporting to smaller employers.

**Joint pay assessment.** A gap of 5% or more in any category, not justified by objective, gender-neutral criteria and not remedied within six months of reporting, triggers a joint pay assessment with worker representatives.

**Enforcement.** The burden of proof shifts to the employer, and workers can recover full compensation, including back pay. An undocumented pay decision is hard to defend.

**What I'd do now:** list each EU country with its implementing law and the date you checked it, remove pay-history questions, build the job evaluation, and run a pay equity analysis with counsel before your first report.
cr-3:
Not necessarily, and not "no" either. A raw gap tells you something real, but it doesn't tell you why.

**What a raw gap measures.** It compares the average pay of all women with all men, regardless of job. A 15% gap usually blends two things:
- **Composition:** women concentrated in lower levels, lower-paid job families, or lower-paid locations
- **Unexplained differences:** women paid less than men in the same job, level and location, with similar experience and performance

Only the second is the classic equal-pay question. But the first isn't automatically innocent: if women are hired at lower levels or promoted more slowly, that's a finding about leveling and promotion, and it can be discriminatory too.

**How to find out**
1. **Set up privilege first.** Decide with employment counsel, before running anything, whether counsel directs the analysis and who sees results.
2. **Run an adjusted analysis.** Regress the log of annualized base pay on legitimate, job-related factors: level, job family, location, time in role, relevant experience. Use performance ratings only if they've passed a bias check. The coefficient on gender gives the adjusted gap. Report it with the sample size and an interval.
3. **Test the controls.** Controlling for level can hide bias in who gets leveled. Compare level at hire, starting pay, and promotion rates by gender.
4. **Look at individuals.** List everyone paid well below what the model predicts for their role and profile, and review them with their managers. With small groups, skip the regression and review people against peers directly.
5. **Fix individuals, not averages.** Fund adjustments for the people flagged, set an effective date, and re-run to confirm.

**What results might look like (illustrative):** a 15% raw gap often shrinks to a few percent after controls. If an adjusted gap of, say, 3% has an interval that excludes zero, that's a signal to review and remediate, not a precise company figure. If it's near zero, look hard at hiring and promotion before concluding all is well.

**Why the raw number still matters.** It's what gets reported: the UK requires it for employers with 250+ employees, and the EU Pay Transparency Directive requires mean and median gaps from 2027 for larger employers. Under the directive, an unexplained gap of 5% or more in a category of workers can trigger a joint pay assessment.

Whether any gap amounts to unlawful discrimination is a legal determination. Compensation view, not legal advice (as of 2026-10-23); take the results to employment counsel.
